column2: For the stated historical 1961-Act context, residential status requires the applicable presence and other statutory tests; foreign citizenship does not by itself establish non-resident tax status.
column3: A foreign passport automatically establishes non-residence even when the person meets the applicable Indian residence tests.

column2: In the historical rules, RNOR scope differs from both ordinary residence and non-residence; certain foreign income from a business controlled in India can enter RNOR scope under the applicable conditions.
column3: RNOR status exempts every foreign-accruing income without considering an India-controlled business or profession set up in India.

column2: A foreign amount first received abroad and later remitted to India is not taxed merely as a fresh Indian first receipt; residence and other charging rules must still be assessed separately.
column3: The later remittance becomes a second first receipt taxable solely because the money enters an Indian bank account.

column2: Qualifying rent from agricultural land situated in India is distinguished from foreign agricultural-land rent for the historical Indian agricultural-income exemption.
column3: All foreign agricultural-land rent qualifies for that Indian exemption because the underlying activity is agricultural.

column2: Income from processing agricultural produce requires examining whether operations and conditions fit the agricultural definition or mixed-income rules; agricultural raw material alone is insufficient.
column3: Every manufactured product made from farm produce gives entirely exempt agricultural income.

column2: Where historical partial-integration conditions apply, exempt agricultural income can influence the rate computation without being included as ordinary taxable income.
column3: The agricultural exemption prevents agricultural income from affecting any rate computation even when partial-integration conditions expressly apply.

column2: Salary already taxed on advance receipt is not taxed again solely when it later becomes due; the timing rule is applied without duplicate inclusion of the same salary.
column3: The later due date requires a second inclusion because salary is chargeable both on receipt and on becoming due.

column2: Monthly fees from independent clients need not be salary; the employer-employee relationship and relevant income-head rules matter more than payment frequency.
column3: A monthly payment schedule alone establishes salary treatment even for an independent professional without employment.

column2: Pension received by the former employee ordinarily belongs to salary, while family pension received by a beneficiary is distinguished under the historical income-head rules.
column3: Family pension is the beneficiary's salary because the deceased employee's employment relationship transfers automatically to the beneficiary.

column2: Subletting receipts of a tenant are not automatically house-property income because that head's ownership requirements differ from merely receiving rent.
column3: Every subletting receipt is house-property income because income-head classification depends only on the payment being called rent.

column2: In a stated eligible historical case, GAV Rs 4,00,000 less qualifying municipal taxes Rs 40,000 actually paid by the owner gives NAV Rs 3,60,000.
column3: The same NAV is obtained by deducting municipal taxes merely accrued but explicitly not paid, irrespective of the historical actual-payment condition.

column2: With NAV Rs 3,60,000 and deductible interest Rs 1,00,000 in the stated historical let-out case, income is Rs 1,52,000 after the 30% NAV deduction.
column3: Those figures give income Rs 2,52,000 because the 30% deduction applies only to the interest rather than NAV.

column2: A business starts with accounting profit but adjusts disallowable expenditure and permissible tax allowances; identical cash payment timing does not make every book expense deductible.
column3: Every expense charged in audited accounts is deductible without further tax adjustment.

column2: A proprietor's personal holiday remains personal on the stated facts even if paid from the business account; the payment source does not create business purpose.
column3: Payment from the business account converts the personal holiday into an ordinary deductible business expense.

column2: Buying a capital asset is not automatically an immediate ordinary revenue deduction; the relevant capital allowance and statutory rules must be examined.
column3: The full purchase price of any depreciable capital asset is automatically deductible as a routine revenue expense in the purchase year.

column2: In a stated historical depreciation block with opening WDV Rs 5,00,000, qualifying additions Rs 1,00,000 and disposal proceeds Rs 80,000, the pre-depreciation block figure is Rs 5,20,000, subject to the stated continuing-block conditions.
column3: The block figure is Rs 6,80,000 because disposal proceeds increase the depreciable base in the continuing block.

column2: Shares genuinely held as business inventory can produce business income, distinguished from investment capital gains; the instrument being a share does not alone settle the head.
column3: Every share-sale surplus is capital gain regardless of the stated inventory classification and business facts.

column2: Given eligible consideration Rs 8,00,000, allowed transfer costs Rs 50,000 and allowable asset cost Rs 5,00,000, stated gain before exemption is Rs 2,50,000.
column3: Those same supplied figures give gain Rs 3,50,000 because transfer costs are added to consideration.

column2: An ordinary business loss cannot offset salary under the historical inter-head restriction, while long-term capital loss is restricted to eligible long-term capital gains.
column3: Ordinary business and long-term capital losses can both offset salary because GTI combines all income heads.

column2: Under historical capital-loss rules, short-term capital loss can offset eligible short- or long-term capital gains, while long-term capital loss cannot offset short-term capital gains.
column3: Both kinds of capital loss can offset only gains with the same holding-period classification.

column2: Historical speculation loss has a restricted set-off route against qualifying speculation profit rather than unrestricted adjustment against ordinary salary or business income.
column3: Calling an activity a business permits its speculation loss to offset every ordinary business profit without special restriction.

column2: Income directly from an asset transferred to a spouse without adequate consideration can be clubbed under the applicable rule, while income on reinvested accumulated income requires distinct analysis.
column3: Once the first asset is transferred, every later independent income of the spouse is automatically clubbed forever.

column2: Historical minor-income clubbing has exceptions for qualifying income from the minor's manual work or skill; passive investment income is a different case.
column3: A minor's qualifying personal-skill earnings must be clubbed solely because the recipient is below majority.

column2: On stipulated fully eligible figures, GTI Rs 4,00,000 and eligible Chapter VI-A amount Rs 5,00,000 cannot create negative total income Rs 1,00,000 under the ordinary GTI ceiling.
column3: The excess deduction automatically creates a carried-forward negative total income Rs 1,00,000.

column2: Using genuine permitted depreciation or lease choices is distinguished from suppressing sales or fabricating invoices; a lower liability alone does not establish unlawful evasion.
column3: Any deliberate lawful choice that reduces tax liability is evasion because the taxpayer intended to save tax.

column2: A fully deductible relevant cash expense Rs 1,000 at a supplied usable 30% tax rate has after-tax cost Rs 700; an unusable deduction would require different treatment.
column3: That deductible expense has after-tax cost Rs 1,300 because the tax rate is added to the payment.

column2: A lease-versus-own comparison must use relevant after-tax cash flows at their dates, including stipulated depreciation, financing and residual-value effects where applicable.
column3: Comparing total undiscounted payments alone gives the same decision regardless of payment timing, depreciation and terminal value.

column2: On a stipulated capped-credit method, Indian tax Rs 30,000 on the same income and qualifying foreign tax Rs 40,000 permit credit Rs 30,000, rather than automatically the full foreign payment.
column3: Those stipulated figures permit Rs 40,000 credit because foreign tax exceeds the Indian tax on the income.

column2: Resale-price method uses a relevant gross resale margin, cost-plus an appropriate gross cost markup, and TNMM a suitable net profit indicator; comparable functions and adjustments matter.
column3: TNMM is simply the resale-price method using a gross margin under a different name.

column2: Final specified tax Rs 90,000 with admissible TDS Rs 40,000 and advance tax Rs 30,000 leaves Rs 20,000 before any other stipulated adjustment.
column3: Those credits increase the remaining payment to Rs 1,60,000 because prepaid taxes are additional taxes rather than credits.
